title: Adjectives and Adverbs: Modifiers at Work

blocks.text: "I only ate two mangoes" and "I ate only two mangoes" contain exactly the same five words. The first says eating was all you did with them; the second says you ate no more than two. Move one modifier and the meaning shifts — which is why examiners love this topic.

blocks.markdown:
Both adjectives and adverbs are **modifiers**: they add information to another word. What separates them is *what* they modify.

- An **adjective** modifies a noun or pronoun: a *diligent* student, the soup is *peppery*.
- An **adverb** modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb: she sang *sweetly*, *extremely* hot, *very* quickly.

So the first question to ask is never "does it end in -ly?" but "which word does this describe?"

blocks.title: -ly is not a reliable test
blocks.text: *Friendly*, *lonely*, *costly* and *cowardly* end in -ly but are adjectives. Meanwhile *fast*, *hard*, *late*, *early* and *well* are adverbs with no -ly at all. Always decide by what the word modifies, not by its ending.

blocks.markdown:
### The linking-verb trap

After a **linking verb** — be, seem, appear, become, remain, look, sound, feel, taste, smell — use an **adjective**, because the word describes the subject:

- The children looked **happy**. (they appeared happy)
- The soup tastes **peppery**.
- She felt **bad** about the delay.

After an **action verb**, use an **adverb**, because the word describes the action:

- She looked at me **happily**.
- He drove **carefully**.

The same verb can be either, so read the sense before you choose.

blocks.caption: Degrees of comparison, including the irregular forms

items: One syllable: add -er and -est — *tall, taller, tallest*.
Two syllables ending in -y: change y to i, then add -er and -est — *happy, happier, happiest*.
Three or more syllables: use *more* and *most* — *beautiful, more beautiful, most beautiful*.
Never combine both methods: *more better* and *most tallest* are double comparatives and always wrong.
Use the comparative for two items and the superlative for three or more.

blocks.title: Repairing a sentence with a badly placed modifier
blocks.prompt: Improve this sentence: "Walking down Balogun Street, the tailor's new signboard caught my eye."

steps.text: Find the modifying phrase. It is *Walking down Balogun Street*, an -ing phrase at the front of the sentence.
A phrase like this always attaches to the subject that follows it. Ask what the subject is: *the tailor's new signboard*.
Read the two together and check the sense: the signboard was walking down the street. That cannot be right, so the modifier is dangling.
Decide who was really walking. It was *I*.
Rewrite so that the doer of the walking is the subject: 'Walking down Balogun Street, I noticed the tailor's new signboard.'
Alternatively, turn the phrase into a full clause: 'As I was walking down Balogun Street, the tailor's new signboard caught my eye.'

blocks.answer: Walking down Balogun Street, I noticed the tailor's new signboard.

blocks.markdown:
### Order of adjectives

When several adjectives modify one noun, English fixes their order:

**opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose**

So we say *a beautiful large old round brown Nigerian wooden carving*, and never *a wooden beautiful carving*. In practice you will rarely stack more than three, but the sequence still applies: the material adjective always sits nearest the noun.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Put a modifier as close as possible to the word it modifies. When a question asks which sentence is correct, check where *only*, *nearly*, *almost* and *even* have been placed — a shifted position is nearly always the planted error.

points: An adjective modifies a noun or pronoun; an adverb modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb.
The -ly ending is unreliable — decide by asking what the word describes.
Use an adjective after a linking verb and an adverb after an action verb.
Short adjectives take -er and -est; longer ones take *more* and *most*, and the two methods are never combined.
The comparative compares two things and the superlative three or more.
Keep every modifier beside the word it modifies to avoid a dangling or misplaced modifier.
